definition: A second-stage retrieval process that re-scores and reorders an initial set of candidate results using a more accurate (often more computationally expensive) model.
details: Re-ranking is commonly used in search and RAG pipelines: a fast, approximate retriever fetches a broad candidate set, and a slower, more precise re-ranker (often a cross-encoder) refines the final ordering.

explainer.lead: Re-ranking lets a system get precise results without paying for precision on every candidate. It matters because it splits retrieval into a cheap wide pass and an expensive narrow one.

tiers.eli5: Think of a librarian who first grabs a big pile of maybe-relevant books, then a slower expert reads them and puts the best ones on top.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers pair a fast approximate retriever with a cross-encoder re-ranker over the top-N candidates. Pitfall: setting the candidate count too low silently caps final quality, since the re-ranker can only reorder what it is given.
tiers.paperLevel: A two-stage ranking: a scorer f(q, d) is computed for each candidate d in an initial set, and results are sorted by that score. Cost scales with the candidate set size, so re-ranking is bounded by the first-stage recall.

explainer.example: A search system retrieves 100 documents with a vector index, then a cross-encoder scores all 100 and the top 10 are shown.
